pos: n. (Roman emperor 379–395, who made Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire and was excommunicated by Ambrose of Milan)
etymology: Greek Theodosios, gift of God. His reign closed the Arian controversy politically and opened a longer question: what happens to a church that the state has adopted.
biblical_def: Theodosius made orthodoxy imperial policy, and in 390 ordered a massacre at Thessalonica; Ambrose refused him communion until he did public penance, and he submitted. Scripture supplies the two halves of that story. The magistrate is God's servant: “he is the minister of God to thee for good… for he beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4), and the church is to be subject to him (Rom 13:1). And the magistrate is under a word he does not control: Nathan said to David, “Thou art the man” (2Sa 12:7). His heart is not his own: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1). And the spheres are distinguished: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines emperor as the sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; and excommunication as the act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the church.
webster_full: EMPEROR, n. The sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; a title of dignity superior to that of king.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of a church, by an ecclesiastical sentence.
PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority, as a punishment for his faults.
scriptures: Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
corruption_summary: State establishment is remembered as the church's victory, and it cost more than it bought.
corruption_paragraphs: The episode with Ambrose is genuinely admirable and should be told first. An emperor who could execute a bishop was refused the sacrament by one, on the ground of blood shed at Thessalonica, and he did public penance. That is a bishop exercising the only authority the church has — a spiritual one — against the greatest power on earth, and winning. It is the exact opposite of the church borrowing the sword, and it is the model the Reformed have pointed to whenever they argued that ecclesiastical and civil authority are distinct.

The longer consequence of establishment is harder to admire. When belonging to the church becomes the path to office and advantage, the church fills with people who have not been converted, discipline weakens because the members are the population, and the state acquires an interest in what is preached. Within a generation of Theodosius the imperial power was being used against heretics, and the precedent set there ran through a thousand years and reached Servetus. A church protected by the sword will eventually be asked to bless it.

The Baptist and wider Reformed answer — a regenerate membership, a distinct spiritual authority, liberty of conscience under a magistrate who has no jurisdiction over the soul — is an answer to this history. It does not despise the magistrate; Romans 13 is unambiguous, and a Christian owes subjection, honour and taxes to rulers far worse than Theodosius. It says only that Caesar's things and God's things are different things, that Christ said so, and that the church loses more than it gains whenever it forgets which it is holding.
roots_summary: Greek exousiai huperechousai (G1849), the higher powers; diakonos theou (G1249), the minister of God; machaira (G3162), the sword; apodote (G591), render.
roots_lines: Greek diakonos theou (G1249) — God's minister, said of the civil magistrate; Romans 13:4 twice.
Greek machaira (G3162) — sword; Romans 13:4 — committed to the magistrate, never to the church.
Greek apodote ta Kaisaros Kaisari (G591) — render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's; Matthew 22:21, Mark 12:17, Luke 20:25.
usage: “He beareth not the sword in vain” — and the sword is the magistrate's.
“Thou art the man” — a prophet, to a king, with no army.
“Unto Caesar… and unto God” — different things.

pos: n. (the name of nine popes; chiefly Boniface VIII, whose bull Unam Sanctam of 1302 declared submission to the Roman pontiff necessary to salvation)
etymology: Latin bonum facere, to do good. The name was also borne by the eighth-century missionary to Germany; Calvin's references are to the popes, and the disputed claim is the one made in 1302.
biblical_def: Boniface VIII asserted that it is altogether necessary to salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman pontiff. Scripture locates that necessity elsewhere: “Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12). It names one Mediator: “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). It gives the church one Head, that “in all things he might have the preeminence” (Col 1:18). It forbids the titles that go with such a claim: “all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). And it forbids the pattern: “it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pope as the bishop of Rome, the head of the Catholic church; and bull as a letter, edict or rescript of the pope, published or transmitted to the churches.
webster_full: POPE, n. The bishop of Rome, the head of the Catholic church.
BULL, n. A letter, edict or rescript of the pope, published or transmitted to the churches over which he is head, containing some decree, order or decision.
It is used chiefly in matters of justice or of grace. If the former, the lead or seal is hung by a hempen cord; if the latter, by a silken thread.
scriptures: Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
corruption_summary: A jurisdiction is made a condition of salvation, and the New Testament attaches salvation to a name rather than an office.
corruption_paragraphs: The claim of Unam Sanctam is not a matter of church order but of soteriology, which is why the Reformers treated it as they did. To say that submission to a particular bishop is necessary to salvation is to add a condition to the gospel, and Galatians establishes what happens to any gospel with an added condition — even circumcision, which God Himself had once commanded. Acts 4:12 is the exclusive claim of the New Testament and it is exclusive about a person: none other name. Adding an office to the name is the same operation Paul anathematised, whoever performs it.

It should be said plainly that Boniface VIII was making a political argument in a quarrel with the king of France, and that the bull's high claims were framed in a losing struggle over taxation and jurisdiction. That is not an excuse; it is a warning about how doctrine gets made. Positions taken to win a dispute have a way of hardening into articles, and every tradition should examine which of its own certainties were forged in a fight rather than found in a text.

The Reformed objection is not to church authority. The 1689 has chapters on officers, discipline and the communion of churches, and treats the local congregation's censures as real. What it denies is a universal jurisdiction attached to a see, and a salvation contingent on it. Colossians 1:18 gives the reason in a single clause: that in all things he might have the preeminence. Any office that requires submission as a term of salvation has taken a preeminence the verse assigns elsewhere.
roots_summary: Greek onoma (G3686), name; mesites (G3316), mediator; kephale (G2776), head; proteuo (G4409), to have the preeminence.
roots_lines: Greek ouk estin en allo oudeni he soteria (G4991) — neither is there salvation in any other; Acts 4:12.
Greek heis mesites (G3316) — one mediator; 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24.
Greek proteuo (G4409) — to hold the first place; Colossians 1:18 only.
usage: “None other name under heaven” — a name, not an office.
“One mediator between God and men” — one, and He is named.
“That in all things he might have the preeminence”.

pos: n. (Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor 161–180, Stoic philosopher, under whose reign Christians were persecuted at Rome and Lyons)
etymology: Latin Aurelius, from aurum, gold. His Meditations are among the noblest writings of the pagan world, and Justin Martyr and the martyrs of Lyons died under his government.
biblical_def: Marcus Aurelius is the case of a virtuous pagan who persecuted the church, and Scripture prepares believers for exactly that. The trial is expected: “think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you” (1Pe 4:12). The Lord had said so: “If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20). The charge to a suffering church is brief: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). His school is named in Scripture, at Athens, among “certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks” (Act 17:18). And the conduct required toward such a ruler is fixed: “pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Mat 5:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stoic as a disciple of Zeno, who held that men should be free from passion, unmoved by joy or grief, and submit without complaint to the unavoidable necessity by which all things are governed.
webster_full: STOIC, n. A disciple of the philosopher Zeno, who founded a sect.
The Stoics held that men should be free from passion, unmoved by joy or grief, and should submit without complaint to the unavoidable necessity by which all things are governed.
STOICAL, a. Pertaining to the Stoics; not affected by passion; unfeeling; manifesting indifference to pleasure or pain.
scriptures: Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you:
John 15:20
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.

Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
Mat 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
corruption_summary: Persecutors are imagined as monsters, and the church's severest test came from a man widely admired for his virtue.
corruption_paragraphs: Aurelius is uncomfortable because he does not fit the picture. He was temperate, dutiful, self-examining and personally decent, and his Meditations are still read for their moral seriousness; and under his government Christians were burned at Lyons and Justin was beheaded at Rome. He appears to have regarded Christian steadfastness under torture as mere obstinacy — the one reference in his book that may touch them dismisses their willingness to die as theatrical. A high pagan virtue looked at martyrdom and saw bad taste.

That is worth holding, because it shows how the world's best moral formation can be blind at precisely the point that matters. Stoicism taught endurance without hope, submission to necessity rather than trust in a Person, and a peace achieved by not caring too much about anything that could be taken away. Christian endurance looks superficially similar and is opposite at the root: it is love of what can be taken, held with an expectation of resurrection. Aurelius's calm was a defence; the martyrs' was a confidence.

First Peter 4:12 is the pastoral instruction and its first word is the useful one: think it not strange. Persecution is not an interruption of the normal Christian condition; it is one of its ordinary forms, and a church surprised by it has been told otherwise by someone. The command in Matthew 5:44 — pray for them which despitefully use you — was given to people under a Roman occupation and is not a figure of speech. Whatever a Christian owes a hostile magistrate, it includes prayer for him, and it does not include hatred.
roots_summary: Greek purosis (G4451), a fiery trial, burning; dioko (G1377), to persecute; Stoikos (G4770), Stoic; stephanos tes zoes (G4735), the crown of life.
roots_lines: Greek purosis (G4451) — a burning, fiery trial; 1 Peter 4:12, Revelation 18:9, 18:18.
Greek Stoikos (G4770) — Stoic; Acts 17:18 only.
Greek stephanos tes zoes (G4735) — crown of life; Revelation 2:10, James 1:12.
usage: “Think it not strange” — the first words of the instruction.
“Be thou faithful unto death” — said to a church under an admired emperor.
“Pray for them which despitefully use you” — and it is not a figure of speech.

pos: adj. (pertaining to an empire or an emperor; sovereign in the highest civil degree)
etymology: Latin imperium, command, dominion. The New Testament was written inside one empire, addressed to subjects of it, and its Lord was executed by its officer.
biblical_def: The imperial power frames the whole New Testament. It sets the scene of the nativity: “there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed” (Luk 2:1). It is invoked against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). It is used by Paul: “I appeal unto Caesar” (Act 25:11). It is penetrated by the gospel: “All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household” (Php 4:22). And it is judged: to the beast “power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations” (Rev 13:7) — given, which is the last word on every empire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imperial as pertaining to an empire or to an emperor; royal; and belonging to a supreme or sovereign power, as imperial authority.
webster_full: IMPERIAL, a. Pertaining to an empire, or to an emperor; as an imperial dominion; imperial city.
2. Royal; belonging to a monarch; as an imperial crown.
3. Pertaining to supreme authority; sovereign; supreme; as imperial power; imperial authority.
IMPERIOUS, a. Commanding; dictatorial; haughty; arrogant; overbearing.
scriptures: Luk 2:1
And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.
John 19:15
But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Caesar.

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar.
Php 4:22
All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household.
Rev 13:7
And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations.
corruption_summary: Political power is treated as ultimate by those who hold it and by those who fear it, and Revelation says it was given.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 2:1 is a study in what the Bible thinks of imperial power. Caesar Augustus, the most powerful man alive, issues a decree that all the world should be taxed — and the effect recorded in Scripture is that it moved a pregnant carpenter's wife eighty miles to the town a prophet had named seven centuries earlier. The emperor is a real cause and he is also an instrument, and he does not know it. That is the perspective Christians are given on political power: entirely real, entirely serious, and not the level at which the decisive things are happening.

John 19:15 is the darkest sentence in the Gospel and it is spoken by the chief priests: We have no king but Caesar. To secure a crucifixion, the custodians of Israel's hope renounced the hope. That is what a captive religious establishment sounds like, and every church that has traded its confession for the protection or approval of a government has said some version of it. The line is worth keeping in mind whenever the church finds itself needing the state's goodwill.

Philippians 4:22 is the counter-image and it is almost a joke. Paul, a prisoner of the empire, closes a letter with greetings from the saints, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household — the slaves and officials of the imperial palace, converted. The gospel got in. Within three centuries the empire that executed its Founder was arguing about His nature at a council, which introduced a different set of problems, but the point stands: Revelation 13:7 says power was given to the beast, and what is given can be withdrawn, and no empire has ever outlasted the church it persecuted.
roots_summary: Greek Kaisar (G2541), Caesar; dogma (G1378), a decree; epikaleomai (G1941), to appeal; edothe auto (G1325), it was given unto him.
roots_lines: Greek dogma (G1378) — a decree; Luke 2:1, Acts 16:4, 17:7, Colossians 2:14.
Greek Kaisara epikaloumai (G1941) — I appeal unto Caesar; Acts 25:11, 25:21, 26:32, 28:19.
Greek edothe auto (G1325) — there was given unto him; Revelation 13:5, 13:7, 13:14–15.
usage: “A decree from Caesar Augustus” — and it moved a woman to Bethlehem.
“We have no king but Caesar” — said by the chief priests.
“They that are of Caesar's household” — from a prisoner of the empire.

pos: n. (the carrying on of a lawsuit; contest in a court of law)
etymology: Latin litigare, to dispute at law, from lis, a lawsuit, and agere, to drive. Paul's word for the practice among Christians is simply to go to law.
biblical_def: Litigation between believers is what Paul confronts at Corinth. He begins with astonishment: “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?” (1Co 6:1). He then concedes the case is already lost whoever wins: “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” (1Co 6:7). The Lord's counsel runs the same way: “if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also” (Mat 5:40); and, “when thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate… give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him” (Luk 12:58).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines litigation as the act or process of carrying on a suit in a court of law or equity; judicial contest; and litigious as inclined to judicial contest, quarrelsome.
webster_full: LITIGATION, n. The act or process of carrying on a suit in a court of law or equity for the recovery of a right or claim; a judicial contest.
LITIGIOUS, a. Inclined to judicial contest; given to the practice of contending in law; quarrelsome; contentious; fond of litigation.
2. Disputable; controvertible; subject to contention.
scriptures: Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?
Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?
Mat 5:40
And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also.

When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, as thou art in the way, give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him; lest he hale thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and the officer cast thee into prison.
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
corruption_summary: Winning is treated as vindication, and Paul says the lawsuit itself is the defeat.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 6:7 is the sentence that dismantles the whole calculation: there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Not because the plaintiff was wrong about the facts — Paul never examines the merits. The existence of the suit is the failure, and it belongs to both parties and to the congregation that could not settle it. The world is watching brothers in a public dispute over money, and no verdict repairs what that has already said about the gospel they claim.

Then come the two questions the church has never wanted: why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? Paul is asking a wronged man to absorb a real loss. That is not naivety about justice — he elsewhere insists on his rights as a citizen, appeals to Caesar, and demands that the magistrates at Philippi come and fetch him out themselves. The distinction is that a believer's own vindication against a brother is the thing he is free to give up, because he has a Judge and a future that make the loss survivable.

The positive instruction is not passivity but process. Verse 5 asks whether there is not a wise man among you who shall be able to judge between his brethren, which assumes the church can and should hear such matters; Matthew 18 gives the escalation, and 1 Timothy 5:19 the evidentiary standard. A congregation with no capacity to settle a dispute between members will drive them to the courts by default. The alternative to litigation is not silence — it is a church that can hear a case.
roots_summary: Greek krino (G2919), to go to law, judge; krima (G2917), a matter for judgment, a fault; adikeo (G91), to suffer wrong; apostereo (G650), to be defrauded.
roots_lines: Greek krinesthai (G2919) — to go to law, be judged; 1 Corinthians 6:1, 6:6, Matthew 5:40.
Greek hettema (G2275) — a fault, a defeat, coming short; 1 Corinthians 6:7, Romans 11:12.
Greek adikeisthe / apostereisthe (G91, G650) — take wrong / suffer defrauding; 1 Corinthians 6:7.
usage: “There is utterly a fault among you” — and the merits are never examined.
“Why do ye not rather take wrong?” — a real loss, absorbed.
“Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you?” — the church should hear it.

pos: v. (to wrest from a man by force, threat or the abuse of an office)
etymology: Latin extorquere, to twist out, from ex-, out, and torquere, to twist. The AV's extortioner is a standing category, and it is listed among sins that bar from the kingdom.
biblical_def: To extort is to twist a thing out of a man. Paul makes the extortioner a case for church discipline: “if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat” (1Co 5:11), and lists the same among those who “shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (1Co 6:10). The Lord finds it inside religious scruple: “ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Mat 23:25). The Pharisee thanks God he is not one (Luk 18:11). And John's counsel to the publicans is exact: “Exact no more than that which is appointed you” (Luk 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines extort as to draw from by force or compulsion; to wrest or wring from by physical force, by menace, duress, authority, or by any illegal means.
webster_full: EXTORT, v.t. To draw from by force or compulsion; to wrest or wring from by physical force, by menace, duress, violence, authority, or by any illegal means.
Conquerors extort contributions from the vanquished.
EXTORTION, n. The act of extorting; the act or practice of wresting any thing from a person by force, duress, menaces, authority, or by any undue exercise of power.
scriptures: But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.
Luk 3:13
And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you.
corruption_summary: Extortion is imagined as a criminal act, and Webster names its ordinary instrument: the undue exercise of power.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's phrase is the one to keep: extortion is wresting a thing from a person by force, duress, menaces, authority, or by any undue exercise of power. The last clause covers most actual cases. The publicans John addressed were not robbers; they held a lawful office with a lawful right to collect, and the extortion consisted in taking more than was appointed while remaining entirely within the system. His counsel to them is correspondingly narrow — not leave your trade, but exact no more than that which is appointed you.

First Corinthians 5:11 is startling for where it puts the extortioner: in a list with the fornicator and the idolater, as a man a church may not eat with. Financial oppression is treated as a disciplinable offence of the same order as sexual sin, which is not how most congregations rank things. An employer squeezing wages, a lender exploiting desperation, a family member using a will as leverage — each is in Paul's category, and each is usually handled in churches as a private matter rather than as a case.

Matthew 23:25 lands it where it is least expected. The scrupulous men who tithed mint and anise are told that within, the cup is full of extortion and excess — the scruple and the extortion in the same person, and the scruple functioning as the cover. That is the commonest form the sin takes among religious people. It does not present as greed; it presents as prudence, as good management, as holding someone to what was agreed, and the man doing it is often the one most confident that his outside is clean.
roots_summary: Greek harpax (G727), an extortioner, a ravener; harpage (G724), extortion, plunder; prasso (G4238), to exact, collect; akrasia (G192), excess.
roots_lines: Greek harpax (G727) — extortioner, rapacious; 1 Corinthians 5:10–11, 6:10, Luke 18:11; and of wolves, Matthew 7:15.
Greek harpage (G724) — extortion, plunder; Matthew 23:25, Luke 11:39, Hebrews 10:34.
Greek meden pleon…prassete (G4238) — exact no more; Luke 3:13.
usage: “Exact no more than that which is appointed you” — keep the office, change the practice.
“With such an one no not to eat” — the extortioner, in that list.
“Within they are full of extortion” — and they tithed mint.

pos: n. pl. (carved or cast likenesses of persons; in worship, the standing images the Law forbids)
etymology: Latin statua, from stare, to stand. The AV's terms are graven image, molten image and standing image; Leviticus 26:1 forbids all three in one verse.
biblical_def: Statues set up for worship are forbidden by name: “Ye shall make you no idols nor graven image, neither rear you up a standing image, neither shall ye set up any image of stone in your land, to bow down unto it” (Lev 26:1); and in the Second Commandment, “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath” (Exo 20:4). Isaiah follows the workman through the whole absurd process (Isa 44:16–17). The psalm gives the verdict: “They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not… they that make them are like unto them” (Psa 115:5–8). And Paul says it at Athens, surrounded by the finest sculpture in the world: “we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Act 17:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines statue as an image; a solid substance formed by carving or casting into the likeness of a living being, and representing a man, a horse or other animal.
webster_full: STATUE, n. An image; a solid substance formed by carving into the likeness of a whole living being; as a statue of Hercules or of a lion.
STATUARY, n. The art of carving images as representatives of real persons or things.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; as an image wrought out of stone, wood or wax.
scriptures: Lev 26:1
Ye shall make you no idols nor graven image, neither rear you up a standing image, neither shall ye set up any image of stone in your land, to bow down unto it: for I am the LORD your God.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not:
They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
corruption_summary: The Second Commandment is read as a ban on art, and it is a ban on worship directed at what a man has made.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed have been careful here and the care is often lost in caricature. The same God who forbade graven images commanded cherubim of gold over the mercy seat, pomegranates and lilies on the pillars, oxen under the brasen sea, and a serpent of brass on a pole. He filled Bezaleel with His Spirit to do the work. The commandment therefore cannot be a prohibition of representational art as such; it forbids images made for worship and images of God Himself, and Deuteronomy 4 gives the reason: at Horeb they saw no similitude, only heard a voice.

The brasen serpent settles what happens to a permitted image over time. It was made at God's command, healing came through it, and Hezekiah broke it in pieces because Israel had begun burning incense to it. That is why the Reformed instinct has been to keep the sanctuary bare of anything that will be venerated — not because beauty is suspect but because the drift is documented and takes about seven centuries in the one case Scripture reports on.

Psalm 115 makes the sharpest point and it is about the worshipper rather than the object. They have mouths and speak not, eyes and see not, ears and hear not — they that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them. A man becomes like what he worships. That is the whole doctrine of idolatry in one line, and it applies well past statuary: whatever a man organises his life around will shape him into its likeness, and a deaf and blind god makes a deaf and blind man.
roots_summary: Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; massekah (H4541), a molten image; matstsebah (H4676), a standing image, pillar; Greek charagma technes (G5480), something graven by art.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesel (H6459) — graven image; Exodus 20:4, Leviticus 26:1, Deuteronomy 4:16, Isaiah 44:9–17.
Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing image, pillar; Leviticus 26:1, Deuteronomy 16:22, 2 Kings 3:2.
Greek charagmati technes kai enthumeseos anthropou (G5480) — graven by art and man's device; Acts 17:29.
usage: “Neither rear you up a standing image” — three kinds, one verse.
“They that make them are like unto them” — the doctrine, in one line.
“Graven by art and man's device” — said in the middle of Athens.

pos: n. (prepared skin used as a writing material; the durable medium of the ancient books)
etymology: From Pergamum in Asia Minor, where the material was developed. The AV has it once, in the last letter Paul wrote: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).
biblical_def: Parchment is the durable writing material of the ancient world. Paul, near his execution, asks for three things: “The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13). Jeremiah's roll was cut and burned by a king, and rewritten: Jehoiakim “cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire” (Jer 36:23); “Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch… who wrote therein… all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire” (Jer 36:32). Job wished for permanence: “Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!” (Job 19:23). And John sees “a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals” (Rev 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines parchment as the skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing; and notes it was so called from Pergamus, where it is said to have been invented.
webster_full: PARCHMENT, n. The skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing.
The best parchments are from Pergamus, in Asia Minor, from which place they take their name.
VELLUM, n. A finer kind of parchment or skin, rendered clear and white for writing.
scriptures: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.

Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.
Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!
Rev 5:1
And I saw in the right hand of him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals.
corruption_summary: The Bible's physical transmission is treated as an embarrassment to its inspiration, and Scripture is entirely open about skins, scribes and burned rolls.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 36 is the chapter to give anyone worried that the Bible came to us through fragile human means, because it says so itself and draws the opposite conclusion. A prophet dictates; a scribe writes; the roll is read to a king; the king cuts it up with a penknife three or four leaves at a time and burns it; and the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah again, saying, Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words. Baruch writes it a second time, and there were added besides unto them many like words. The medium is destructible and the word is not.

Second Timothy 4:13 is the most human sentence in the New Testament and it belongs beside all this. Paul is in a Roman prison, expecting to die, and he asks for a cloak because it is cold, and for the books, but especially the parchments. Nobody knows what they were — his own copies of the Scriptures, most likely, perhaps notes or documents. What is certain is that a man at the end of a life like his still wanted to read, and thought the request worth putting in an inspired letter.

The doctrinal use is a caution against two errors. The first treats the text as though it descended without a history, and is then shaken by any manuscript question. The second treats the history as evidence against the doctrine. Scripture itself is unembarrassed: it names the scribes, records the burning, notes the second roll, and asks for the parchments. God's superintendence worked through skins and copyists and a prisoner's request, which is exactly the way He does everything else.
roots_summary: Greek membrana (G3200), parchment; biblion (G975), a book, scroll; Hebrew megillah (H4039), a roll; ta'ar hassopher (H8593), the scribe's penknife.
roots_lines: Greek membrana (G3200) — parchment; 2 Timothy 4:13 only.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — roll, scroll; Jeremiah 36:2, 36:23, 36:28, 36:32, Ezekiel 2:9, Zechariah 5:1.
Greek biblion (G975) — book, scroll; Revelation 5:1–9, 2 Timothy 4:13, John 20:30.
usage: “The books, but especially the parchments” — asked for from a death cell.
“Cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire” — and it was written again.
“Oh that my words were now written!” — and they were.

pos: v. (to laugh at in contempt; to turn a man into a joke in order to dismiss him)
etymology: Latin deridere, to laugh down, from de-, down, and ridere, to laugh. Derision is the argument of those who have none, and Scripture records it being used on Christ twice in one day.
biblical_def: To deride is to laugh a thing down. The Pharisees do it when the Lord teaches about money: “the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him” (Luk 16:14). The rulers do it at the cross: “And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself” (Luk 23:35). The psalm foretold it: “All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head” (Psa 22:7). It is the last stage of a nation's refusal: they “mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people” (2Ch 36:16). And it begins early in Scripture, with Ishmael mocking (Gen 21:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deride as to laugh at in contempt; to turn to ridicule or make sport of; to mock; to treat with scorn by laughter.
webster_full: DERIDE, v.t. To laugh at in contempt; to turn to ridicule or make sport of; to mock; to treat with scorn by laughter.
The wicked deride the righteous.
DERISION, n. The act of laughing at in contempt.
2. Contempt manifested by laughter; scorn.
3. An object of derision or contempt; a laughing-stock.
scriptures: And the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him.
And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself, if he be Christ, the chosen of God.
Psa 22:7
All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,
But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.
Gen 21:9
And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which she had born unto Abraham, mocking.
corruption_summary: Derision is treated as harmless because it is only laughter, and Scripture places it at the end of the road to judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 16:14 gives the mechanism with unusual precision, and the causal clause is doing the work: the Pharisees who were covetous heard all these things, and they derided him. The teaching had landed. Derision was not a failure to understand the parable of the unjust steward; it was a defence against having understood it. That is what mockery usually is — a way of disposing of a claim without answering it, available to anyone, requiring no argument, and it works best on exactly the truths that are most costly to accept.

Second Chronicles 36:16 puts derision in a sequence that ends badly, and each verb is a stage: they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy. Mocking comes first and is the cheapest; despising the words is next; misusing the prophets is last. A culture that has begun to find the message funny is further along that road than it knows, and the same is true of an individual.

The consolation is at the cross, and it is not sentimental. The rulers derided Him with an argument that was formally correct — He saved others, He could have saved Himself — and He did not answer it. Psalm 22 had described the shooting out of the lip and the shaking of the head a thousand years before, and the same psalm ends with all the ends of the world remembering and turning unto the LORD. Any believer laughed at for his faith is standing in a well-documented place, and it is not the place the account ends.
roots_summary: Greek ekmukterizo (G1592), to turn up the nose at, deride; empaizo (G1702), to mock; Hebrew laag (H3932), to deride, scorn; tsachaq (H6711), to laugh, mock.
roots_lines: Greek ekmukterizo (G1592) — to deride, literally to turn up the nose; Luke 16:14, 23:35 — both occurrences.
Hebrew laag (H3932) — to deride, mock; Psalm 22:7, 2 Chronicles 30:10, Nehemiah 2:19, Proverbs 1:26.
Hebrew tsachaq (H6711) — to laugh, mock; Genesis 21:9, and the root of Isaac's name, 21:6.
usage: “Who were covetous… and they derided him” — the teaching had landed.
“They shoot out the lip, they shake the head” — written a thousand years before.
“They mocked the messengers of God” — the first verb in a sequence.

pos: adj. (angry at what is unworthy or unjust; roused by an offence against right)
etymology: Latin indignari, to regard as unworthy, from in-, not, and dignus, worthy. Indignation is anger with a judgment inside it: this ought not to be.
biblical_def: Indignation is anger at what is unworthy, and the Lord shows it. When the disciples turn away the children, “Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me” (Mar 10:14). In the synagogue, faced with men watching to see whether He would heal on the sabbath, He “looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts” (Mar 3:5) — anger and grief together. In the temple He made a scourge of small cords and drove out the changers (John 2:15). At Athens “his spirit was stirred in him” (Act 17:16). And the rule for believers admits the emotion and bounds it: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath” (Eph 4:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indignant as affected at once with anger and disdain; feeling the mingled emotions of wrath and scorn or contempt, as when a person is exasperated at a mean action.
webster_full: INDIGNANT, a. Affected at once with anger and disdain; feeling the mingled emotions of wrath and scorn or contempt, as when a person is exasperated at one who is guilty of a mean action.
INDIGNATION, n. Anger or extreme anger, mingled with contempt, disgust or abhorrence.
2. The anger of a superior; extreme anger; particularly, the wrath of God against sinful men for their ingratitude and rebellion.
scriptures: But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
Mar 3:5

And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.
John 2:15
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;
Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry.
Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
corruption_summary: All anger is treated as sin, and the Lord was angry; and one's own temper is called righteous indignation, and it usually is not.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 3:5 is the verse that settles the first error, and its two clauses must be kept together: He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts. Anger and grief in the same look. That is the signature of righteous indignation and it is the test to apply to one's own: does it come with sorrow for the people it is aimed at? Anger that is enjoyed, that has no grief in it, that would be disappointed if the offender repented, is not what Mark is describing however just its occasion.

The second error is commoner and more comfortable. A great deal of what calls itself righteous indignation is ordinary temper with a doctrinal pretext, and the tells are consistent: it is aroused most reliably by offences against oneself, it is disproportionate, it lasts, and it enjoys company. Ephesians 4:26 supplies a blunt practical limit that cuts through the self-assessment — let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Whatever the anger's merits, it has a curfew, and an indignation that survives the night is being kept for other reasons.

Mark 10:14 is worth noting for what provoked it. The one recorded occasion where the Lord is displeased with His own disciples is when they hindered children from coming to Him — not a doctrinal error, not a scandal, but officiousness that got between people and Christ. Anyone whose ministry involves gatekeeping should sit with that. The offences that move Him in the Gospels are consistently these: hardness toward the suffering, obstruction of the weak, and the turning of His Father's house into a market.
roots_summary: Greek aganakteo (G23), to be much displeased, indignant; orge (G3709), anger; sullupeomai (G4818), to be grieved with; paroxuno (G3947), to be stirred, provoked.
roots_lines: Greek aganakteo (G23) — to be indignant, much displeased; Mark 10:14, Matthew 21:15, 26:8, Luke 13:14.
Greek met' orges…sullupoumenos (G3709, G4818) — with anger, being grieved; Mark 3:5.
Greek paroxuneto (G3947) — was stirred, provoked; Acts 17:16, 1 Corinthians 13:5.
usage: “With anger, being grieved” — both, in one look.
“He was much displeased” — at disciples hindering children.
“Let not the sun go down upon your wrath” — it has a curfew.
